posts.title: Luxury’s next challenge in Latin America isn’t the shelf. It’s protecting it.
posts.sub: Security, traceability and authenticity are becoming part of the commercial infrastructure of a maturing luxury market.
posts.body:
Latin America is building an increasingly sophisticated market for luxury. As more value moves through ports, airports, distribution centres, boutiques and digital platforms, one question grows in importance for maisons: how do you preserve the integrity of a product between creation and consumer?

On 23–24 September 2026, around 80 representatives from 27 countries took part in INTERPOL’s Americas Regional Conference in Georgetown, Guyana. Discussions addressed transnational organised crime, illicit financial flows and emerging threats that cross borders. The meeting reinforced the importance of cooperation and information-sharing among the region’s authorities.

On another front, the World Customs Organization released the results of Operation FRONPIAS, carried out in January 2025 with the participation of 14 customs administrations across the Americas and the Caribbean. The operation recorded the seizure of 13,837,275 items linked to intellectual property, health and safety violations. The figure requires context: 89% of the seized pieces, by volume, were tobacco products. Even so, the initiative illustrates the scale and cross-border nature of customs efforts against counterfeit, substandard or illicit goods.

These developments help explain why asset protection has moved from a peripheral concern to a central one for companies working with high-value goods. The Inter-American Development Bank estimated that the direct costs of crime and violence amounted to 3.44% of GDP in Latin America and the Caribbean in 2022. The estimate includes, among other components, business mitigation spending, public expenditure and human-capital losses. It is an economic indicator: the costs of prevention, loss and uncertainty can influence productivity, investment and operating conditions.

For a maison, entering a territory involves far more than moving goods. It involves intellectual property, reputation, pricing policy, inventory, data, distribution channels and the relationship of trust built with the consumer. In luxury perfumery, these elements make concrete a set of questions that run across the entire chain: how is inventory controlled between importer, warehouse and retailer? How are batches traced? How are diversions into unauthorised channels identified? How is product authenticity verified? How are sell-in, sell-out and reorders tracked? And how can a brand, often far from the local market, see what is actually happening in the territory?

These questions do not turn distributors into security companies. They broaden what is expected of a commercial partner. Capital, retail coverage, marketing and execution capability remain essential — but they now need to be assessed alongside warehouse processes, inventory discipline, traceability, intellectual-property protection, supply-chain security, channel governance and data quality.

It is at this intersection between market development and governance that FÊNIX is incorporating criteria of security, authenticity, traceability, inventory control, channel-diversion prevention and data governance into how operators are evaluated in Latin America. The aim is to understand not only who can import and sell, but also which structures make it possible to preserve value, consistency and trust as a brand grows.

FÊNIX is conducting a regional review with operators, distributors and retailers across different Latin American markets — mapping existing practices, identifying gaps and understanding how centuries-old houses, independent maisons and artistic perfumery projects can develop regional presence with greater control and predictability. This is an ongoing evaluation agenda, not a finished regional standard.

As the market matures, security, authenticity and traceability cease to be mere support functions. They become part of the experience, the reputation and the protection of brand value. The challenge is not to look at Latin America through the lens of risk, but to recognise the infrastructure required for luxury’s growth to be sustainable.

Latin America does not simply need to receive more luxury. It needs to build the infrastructure capable of protecting it as it grows.

Marcelo Capote is founder, CEO & President of FÊNIX. A graduate in Public Relations with a postgraduate degree in Luxury Brand Management in London, he works on developing the luxury and perfumery industry in Latin America and on creating methodologies and technologies applied to retail, market development and international expansion.
